claim: A multicellular organism is able to maintain its complex morphology despite continual renewal and damages.
source: Despite continual renewal and damages, a multicellular organism is able to maintain its complex morphology.
evidence: This is a general statement about biological systems presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Diverging protein sequences can result in similar morphologies.
source: Looking for answers at protein level may be limiting as diverging protein sequences can result in similar morphologies.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to examples of phenotypic plasticity and convergent evolution in the introduction.

claim: Apical-basal and planar cell polarity play progressive roles in development.
source: Inspired by the progressive role of apical-basal and planar cell polarity in development, we propose that stability, complexity, and diversity are emergent properties in populations of proliferating polarized cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction discussing the role of AB polarity and PCP in development.

claim: Stability, complexity, and diversity are emergent properties in populations of proliferating polarized cells.
source: Inspired by the progressive role of apical-basal and planar cell polarity in development, we propose that stability, complexity, and diversity are emergent properties in populations of proliferating polarized cells.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the paper, supported by the theoretical modeling results presented throughout.

claim: The strength of polar adhesion is a major determinant of morphological diversity and stability.
source: our theoretical tool suggests experimentally testable predictions pointing to the strength of polar adhesion, restricted directions of cell polarities, and the rate of cell proliferation to be major determinants of morphological diversity and stability.
evidence: This prediction is based on the modeling results shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Restricted directions of cell polarities are major determinants of morphological diversity and stability.
source: our theoretical tool suggests experimentally testable predictions pointing to the strength of polar adhesion, restricted directions of cell polarities, and the rate of cell proliferation to be major determinants of morphological diversity and stability.
evidence: This prediction is based on the modeling results shown in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: The rate of cell proliferation is a major determinant of morphological diversity and stability.
source: our theoretical tool suggests experimentally testable predictions pointing to the strength of polar adhesion, restricted directions of cell polarities, and the rate of cell proliferation to be major determinants of morphological diversity and stability.
evidence: This prediction is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adult salamander can regenerate entire limbs.
source: Adult salamander can regenerate entire limbs (Eguchi et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eguchi et al., 2011.

claim: During development, some regions can maintain patterning when moved to different parts of an embryo or if the size is varied.
source: during development, some regions can maintain patterning when moved to different parts of an embryo or if the size is varied (Lyons et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lyons et al., 2012.

claim: Morphological similarity may not couple to protein sequence similarity.
source: Examples of phenotypic plasticity (Libby and Rainey, 2011), convergent evolution, and contrasting rates of morphological and protein evolution (Cherry et al., 1979) show that morphological similarity may not couple to the protein sequence similarity (Gould, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to examples of phenotypic plasticity, convergent evolution, and contrasting evolutionary rates.

claim: During early development, the increase in morphological complexity coincides with the progressive polarization of cells.
source: During early development, the increase in morphological complexity coincides with the progressive polarization of cells – first apical-basal (AB) polarity and then planar cell polarity (PCP) (Müller and Bossinger, 2003; Roignot et al., 2013; Andrew and Ewald, 2010; Li and Bowerman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to developmental biology literature.

claim: The developmental progression from morula to blastula to gastrulation is ubiquitous across vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: This theme is ubiquitous across vertebrates and invertebrates (Figure 1): starting from the single fertilized egg cell, first the morula formed by non-polarized cells turns into the blastula – a hollow sphere of cells with AB polarity.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1 and general developmental biology knowledge.

claim: In sea urchin development, a lumen forms in the center of the morula and expands as cells proliferate and rearrange into a hollow sphere.
source: At the morula stage, a lumen in the center is formed and is gradually expanding as cells proliferate and rearrange into the hollow sphere.
evidence: This is a description of sea urchin development based on established knowledge.

claim: During sea urchin gastrulation, a group of cells invaginate and rearrange into a tube that narrows and elongates primarily by cell rearrangement and convergent extension movements.
source: Next, during gastrulation, a group of cells invaginate and rearrange into a tube that narrows and elongates primarily by cell rearrangement and convergent extension movements (Martik and McClay, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martik and McClay, 2017.

claim: PCP drives both invagination and tube elongation in sea urchin gastrulation.
source: Emerging data suggest that PCP drives both invagination and tube elongation (Nishimura et al., 2012; Croce et al., 2006; Long et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Mutations in PCP pathways produce shorter and wider tubes.
source: Mutations in PCP pathways produce shorter and wider tubes (Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2012; Saburi et al., 2008; Kunimoto et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Mutations in PCP pathways produce shorter and wider somites.
source: Mutations in PCP pathways produce shorter and wider tubes (Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2012; Saburi et al., 2008; Kunimoto et al., 2017), somites (Song et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2010.

claim: Mutations in PCP pathways produce shorter and wider embryos.
source: Mutations in PCP pathways produce shorter and wider tubes (Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2012; Saburi et al., 2008; Kunimoto et al., 2017), somites (Song et al., 2010), and embryos (Gong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gong et al., 2004.

claim: Formation and elongation of tubes can proceed without cell division and cell death by cells rearranging along the tube's axis, termed convergent extension.
source: Formation and elongation of the tubes can proceed without cell division and cell death by cells rearranging along the tube's axis, termed convergent extension (CE) (Andrew and Ewald, 2010; Tanimizu et al., 2009; Martik and McClay, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The importance of PCP in gastrulation and tubulogenesis is well established.
source: While the importance of PCP in gastrulation and tubulogenesis is well established (Andrew and Ewald, 2010; Tanimizu et al., 2009; Martik and McClay, 2017; Kunimoto et al., 2017), it is unclear how polarity may control tube morphology.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: It is unclear how polarity may control tube morphology.
source: While the importance of PCP in gastrulation and tubulogenesis is well established (Andrew and Ewald, 2010; Tanimizu et al., 2009; Martik and McClay, 2017; Kunimoto et al., 2017), it is unclear how polarity may control tube morphology.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The bulk-lumens-folds/tubes transition seen across animal species in early embryogenesis is also a key feature of later organ formation.
source: The bulk-lumens-folds/tubes transition seen across animal species in early embryogenesis, is also a key feature of the later organ formation.
evidence: This is based on general developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Early stages of organogenesis in the liver, kidney, brain, gut, and pancreas can be recapitulated in vitro.
source: The early stages of organogenesis in the liver, kidney, brain, gut, and pancreas are apparently so robust, that they can be recapitulated in vitro, allowing for advanced quantification and manipulation (Little, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Little, 2017.

claim: Cells in in vitro pancreatic organoids first grow as a bulk and later acquire AB polarity and develop lumens.
source: Cells in in vitro pancreatic organoids first grow as a bulk and later acquire AB polarity and develop lumens.
evidence: This is based on observations of pancreatic organoid development.

claim: Depending on the growth conditions, pancreatic organoids develop into a hollow sphere or acquire a complex folded shape.
source: Depending on the growth conditions, organoids develop into a hollow sphere or acquire a complex folded shape (Greggio et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Greggio et al., 2013.

claim: It is currently unknown what drives the transition from sphere to folded state in pancreatic organoids.
source: It is currently unknown what drives the transition from sphere to folded state; the two possible hypotheses are rapid proliferation or physical pressure from growing into a stiff matrigel.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Cells are approximated by point particles in the model.
source: Cells are approximated by point particles
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: The point particle approximation allows a substantial gain in computation time compared to vertex-based models.
source: This allows a substantially gain in computation time compared to vertex-based models where cell surface adhesion is explicitly considered (Alt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of computational efficiency with citation to vertex-based models.

claim: In the model, cells interact with a subset of Voronoi neighbors.
source: Interacting neighbors of cell i are selected from a subset of cells sharing a Voronoi surface.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: The line of sight constraint effectively corrects for the finite volume associated with point particles.
source: This constrain effectively corrects for the finite volume associated with point particles and assures that two cells will not interact if the line of sight between their centers is separated by a surface of a third cell.
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling approach.

claim: Without the line of sight constraint, the macroscopic morphologies collapse.
source: Without this constraint, the macroscopic morphologies collapse.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results.

claim: The model results are robust to replacing the line of sight constraint with full Voronoi and a cut-off distance for attraction force.
source: However, our results are robust to replacing the line of sight constraint with full Voronoi and a cut-off distance for attraction force (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the model, AB polarity and PCP are assumed to be orthogonal.
source: We assume that AB polarity and PCP are orthogonal, and that the polarities of one cell align with the polarities of its neighbor cells.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: In the model, the polarities of one cell align with the polarities of its neighbor cells.
source: We assume that AB polarity and PCP are orthogonal, and that the polarities of one cell align with the polarities of its neighbor cells.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: In an epithelial sheet, AB polarities align parallel to each other and tight adherens junctions form in the plane perpendicular to AB polarity.
source: To capture that in an epithelial sheet, AB polarities align parallel to each other and tight adherens junctions form in the plane perpendicular to AB polarity, we introduce the quadruple product
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of epithelial cell biology.

claim: Two interacting cells with AB polarity are maximally attracted if the two apical sides are next to each other.
source: This makes two interacting cells with AB polarity maximally attracted (S1 = 1) if the two apical sides are next to each other.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior based on the mathematical formulation.

claim: If apical side of one cell is next to the basal side of another cell, the two cells will be maximally repulsing.
source: On the other hand, if apical side of one cell is next to the basal side of another cell, the two cells will be maximally repulsing (S1 = −1), see Figure 2A.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior based on the mathematical formulation and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The assumption that two cells with PCP are maximally attracted if their PCP are parallel and cells have the same kind of pole next to each other makes neighbor exchange on a sheet possible and results in convergent extension.
source: We later show that this assumption makes neighbor exchange on a sheet possible and results in CE.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model that is later demonstrated in the results.

claim: Preferred directional adhesion with PCP is not as well established as with AB polarity.
source: However, unlike with tight junctions, preferred directional adhesion with PCP is not as well established.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Both proteins regulating adherens junctions and adherence proteins forming adherens junctions can be planar polarized.
source: Both proteins regulating adherens junctions, for example Smash (Beati et al., 2018), as well as adherence proteins forming adherens junctions can be planar polarized, for example Bazooka, E-cadherins (Simões et al., 2010; Tamada et al., 2017; Levayer and Lecuit, 2013; Warrington et al., 2013; Aigouy and Le Bivic, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: In a sheet of cells, turning AB polarity in one cell will cause a force on its neighbors.
source: One of the implications of the coupling between position and polarity is that in a sheet of cells, turning AB polarity in one cell will cause a force on its neighbors.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model formulation.

claim: In case of two cells, the pair relaxes the imposed stress by rotating both the polarity and their positions.
source: In case of two cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—video 1), the pair relaxes the imposed stress by rotating both the polarity and their positions.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—video 1.

claim: Turning AB polarity in one cell of an epithelial sheet will induce bending of the sheet as is the case with bottle cells in invagination.
source: In biological terms, turning AB polarity in one cell (e.g. by apical constriction, illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2) of an epithelial sheet will induce bending of the sheet as is the case with bottle cells in invagination.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells can acquire PCP without AB polarity present.
source: First, cells can acquire PCP without AB polarity present (Baer et al., 2009; Zorn and Wells, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Proteins required for AB polarity can be planar-polarized.
source: Second, proteins required for AB polarity can be planar-polarized (Warrington et al., 2013; Aigouy and Le Bivic, 2016; Beati et al., 2018; Choi and Sokol, 2009; Dollar et al., 2005; Kaplan and Tolwinski, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Changes in cell shapes during invagination are regulated by PCP in neural tube closure.
source: Third, changes in cell shapes during invagination (e.g. sliding of adherens junctions and formation of bottle cells) are regulated by PCP in neural tube closure (Ossipova et al., 2014; Nishimura et al., 2012; Kinoshita et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Changes in cell shapes during invagination are regulated by PCP in gastrulation in C. elegans.
source: Third, changes in cell shapes during invagination (e.g. sliding of adherens junctions and formation of bottle cells) are regulated by PCP in neural tube closure (Ossipova et al., 2014; Nishimura et al., 2012; Kinoshita et al., 2008), gastrulation in C. elegans (Lee et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2006.

claim: Changes in cell shapes during invagination are regulated by PCP in sea urchin gastrulation.
source: Third, changes in cell shapes during invagination (e.g. sliding of adherens junctions and formation of bottle cells) are regulated by PCP in neural tube closure (Ossipova et al., 2014; Nishimura et al., 2012; Kinoshita et al., 2008), gastrulation in C. elegans (Lee et al., 2006), sea urchin (Croce et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Croce et al., 2006.

claim: Changes in cell shapes during invagination are regulated by PCP in Xenopus gastrulation.
source: Third, changes in cell shapes during invagination (e.g. sliding of adherens junctions and formation of bottle cells) are regulated by PCP in neural tube closure (Ossipova et al., 2014; Nishimura et al., 2012; Kinoshita et al., 2008), gastrulation in C. elegans (Lee et al., 2006), sea urchin (Croce et al., 2006), and Xenopus (Choi and Sokol, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Choi and Sokol, 2009.

claim: When starting a bulk of cells with AB polarities pointing randomly, an initial rapid expansion stabilizes into a complex morphology of interconnected channels.
source: When starting a bulk of cells with AB polarities pointing randomly, an initial rapid expansion (Figure 3A–C) stabilizes into a complex morphology of interconnected channels (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The shape of the complex morphology remains unchanged for at least 10 times longer than the initial expansion.
source: The shape remains unchanged for at least 10 times longer than the initial expansion (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The stability of the shape is illustrated by the time evolution of the average energy per cell that after an initial fast drop converges to a constant value.
source: The stability of the shape is illustrated by the time evolution of the average energy per cell (Figure 3F) that after an initial fast drop converges to a constant value.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3F.

claim: The final energy value is higher than the energy of a hollow sphere.
source: As expected, this value is higher than the energy of a hollow sphere (yellow dot in Figure 3F) – a configuration obtained if we start with radially, instead of random, polarized cells and preserve radial polarization at all times.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3F.

claim: The observed behavior is not sensitive to the shape of the potential.
source: The observed behavior is not sensitive to the shape of the potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The observed behavior is sensitive to how the neighborhood is defined.
source: The observed behavior is not sensitive to the shape of the potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) but is sensitive to how the neighborhood is defined (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Rerunning the simulation with different initial conditions results in a different stable shape.
source: Rerunning the simulation in Figure 3 with different initial conditions results in a different stable shape (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The macroscopic features of the shapes are robust to noise.
source: The macroscopic features of the shapes are robust to noise (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: While the shapes emerging under high and low noise are not identical, the relative position and sizes of the majority of channels and lumens are preserved.
source: While the shapes emerging under high and low noise are not identical, the relative position and sizes of the majority of channels and lumens are preserved.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results shown in the figures.

claim: The changes caused by noise stem from perturbations during initial expansion stage.
source: The changes caused by noise stem from perturbations during initial expansion stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: If the same level of noise is applied after the system reached stable state, noise does not cause any major macroscopic changes.
source: If the same level of noise is applied after the system reached stable state, after time t = 10000, noise does not cause any major macroscopic changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The obtained shapes have self-sealing features.
source: The obtained shapes have self-sealing features, as an initial cut and unwrapping of a section of a surface refolds and seals back into the original morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The shapes are robust to overall growth, retaining the same macroscopic features, just scaled to a larger size.
source: Furthermore, the shapes (Figure 3D–E) are also robust to overall growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F) retaining the same macroscopic features, just scaled to a larger size.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: The orientation of polarities in a subpopulation of cells may be set by the environment that the cells are embedded in.
source: The orientation of polarities in a subpopulation of cells may be set by the environment that the cells are embedded in, for example signaling molecules deposited into extracellular matrix can influence orientation of the AB polarity (Overeem et al., 2015) or signals from neighboring cells of a different type can orient PCP (Chu and Sokol, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: When polarities are fixed and point radially out from the center of mass, a hollow sphere emerges.
source: As anticipated, the difference in symmetries of boundary conditions results in a sphere, a cylinder, or two parallel planes (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: When polarities are fixed and point radially out from a central axis, a hollow tube is obtained.
source: As anticipated, the difference in symmetries of boundary conditions results in a sphere, a cylinder, or two parallel planes (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: When polarities are fixed and point away from a central plane, two flat planes pointing in opposite directions are obtained.
source: As anticipated, the difference in symmetries of boundary conditions results in a sphere, a cylinder, or two parallel planes (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: For all three symmetric initial conditions, if the polarities are allowed to change dynamically and the noise is high, the resulting shape consists of three nested 'Russian doll'-like hollow spheres.
source: At the same time, in these symmetric cases, the differences in initial conditions but without imposed boundary conditions are not sufficient to generate different structures; they all converge to the nested 'Russian doll'-like hollow spheres (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4D.

claim: Polar adhesion enables stable and robust macroscopic shapes.
source: Our results thus support the idea that polar adhesion enables stable and robust macroscopic shapes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: If proliferation is slow, and the time between two cell divisions anywhere in the system is longer than relaxation time of the whole system, the system approaches global equilibrium and will expand as a sphere.
source: If proliferation is slow, and the time between two cell divisions anywhere in the system is longer than relaxation time of the whole system (the time it takes to reach equilibrium), the system approaches global equilibrium and will expand as a sphere.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model.

claim: If proliferation is increased, the system will be pushed out of equilibrium and folds will emerge.
source: However, if proliferation is increased, the system will be pushed out of equilibrium and folds will emerge (Figure 5A, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A.

claim: As cells divide faster, the model predicts a transition from a smooth spherical shell to an increasingly folded structure with multiple pronounced folds.
source: As cells divide faster, our simulations predict a transition from a smooth spherical shell to an increasingly folded structure with multiple pronounced folds, in line with the observation of brain organoids proliferating at different rates (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results in Figure 5A, supported by citation to Li et al., 2017.

claim: External pressure alone can drive folding.
source: While we find that the external pressure is not necessary for folding, pressure alone can also drive folding (Figure 5B, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B.

claim: The pressure-driven folding scenario contradicts the observation that pancreatic organoids can grow as spheres or folded morphologies in gels with the same stiffness but different media composition.
source: However, this scenario contradicts the observation that pancreatic organoids can grow as spheres or folded morphologies in gels with the same stiffness but different media composition (Greggio et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Greggio et al., 2013.

claim: In the pressure-driven case, the number of local minima will reach an upper limit as organoids increase in size.
source: Our simulations predict that in the pressure-driven case, the number of local minima will reach an upper limit as organoids increase in size (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the case of out-of-equilibrium proliferation, new folds can continue forming as organoids grow.
source: In the case of out-of-equilibrium proliferation, new folds can continue forming as organoids grow (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increased proliferation causes more and shallower folds.
source: Increased proliferation causes more and shallower folds.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pressure causes fewer but deeper minima than growth-induced folding.
source: These folds are different than obtained with pressure which causes fewer but deeper minima.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the depth and the horizontal extension of the folds are about double as large with pressure than with growth-induced folding.
source: Quantitatively, both the depth and the horizontal extension of the folds are about double as large with pressure than with growth-induced folding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: It remains unresolved whether oriented cell division or the extent of convergent extension controls tube length and width.
source: Despite the numerous evidences supporting the role of PCP in tubulogenesis, it remains unresolved whether oriented cell division or the extent of CE controls tube length and width (Karner et al., 2009; Carroll and Yu, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: It is debated if it is important for the tubes to maintain regular shape, or if it is only important for tube initiation and growth.
source: It is also debated if it is important for the tubes to maintain regular shape, or if it is only important for tube initiation and growth (Kunimoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Inducing PCP in a spherical lumen leads to global ordering of PCPs parallel to an emerging equator that self-organizes around the sphere.
source: Inducing PCP in a spherical lumen leads to two significant events. First, independent of initial orientation, after some transient time PCPs becomes globally ordered and point in direction parallel to an emerging equator that self-organizes around the sphere (inset in Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: Cells start intercalating along the axis perpendicular to PCP orientation, gradually elongating the lumen.
source: Second, cells start intercalating along the axis perpendicular to PCP orientation, gradually elongating the lumen (Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—video 1.

claim: During intercalations, cells exchange their neighbors through T1-like transitions as reported experimentally.
source: During intercalations, cells exchange their neighbors through T1-like transitions as reported experimentally, Figure 6—figure supplement 3 (Nishimura et al., 2012; Sanchez-Corrales et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The intercalations along the axis continue until the force balance between AB polarity and PCP is restored at a new equilibrium.
source: The intercalations along the axis continue until the force balance between AB polarity and PCP is restored at a new equilibrium.
evidence: This is based on the model dynamics.

claim: The model predicts that the strength of PCP relative to AB polarity determines the width and the length of the tube.
source: Thus, our model predicts that the strength of PCP (λ3) relative to AB polarity (λ1) determines the width and the length of the tube (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Similar tube formation results are obtained if PCP is constrained to always remain in the apical plane and thus does not allow PCP to reorient AB polarity.
source: We obtain similar results if we constrain PCP to always remain in the apical plane and thus does not allow PCP to reorient AB polarity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Combining AB polarization and a local induction of PCP in a subpopulation of cells was sufficient to obtain main stages of sea urchin gastrulation: invagination, tube formation, and elongation through convergent extension as well as merging of the tube with the animal pole.
source: Combining AB polarization and a local induction of PCP in a subpopulation of cells was sufficient to obtain main stages of sea urchin gastrulation: invagination, tube formation, and elongation through CE as well as merging of the tube with the animal pole at the top of the blastula.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: Sea urchin gastrulation consists of primary invagination, driven by swelling of the inner layer of extracellular matrix beneath invaginating cells and formation of a ring of bottle cells due to apical constriction.
source: The current understanding is that sea urchin gastrulation consists of primary invagination, driven by swelling of the inner layer of extracellular matrix beneath invaginating cells (Lane et al., 1993), and formation of a ring of bottle cells due to apical constriction (Kimberly and Hardin, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lane et al., 1993 and Kimberly and Hardin, 1998.

claim: Sea urchin gastrulation includes secondary invagination where tube elongates due to convergent extension.
source: The current understanding is that sea urchin gastrulation consists of primary invagination, driven by swelling of the inner layer of extracellular matrix beneath invaginating cells (Lane et al., 1993), and formation of a ring of bottle cells due to apical constriction (Kimberly and Hardin, 1998), and secondary invagination where tube elongates due to CE (Lyons et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lyons et al., 2012.

claim: PCP is necessary for both invagination, possibly through its effect on apical constriction in bottle cells, and tube extension.
source: PCP is necessary for both invagination, possibly through its effect on apical constriction in bottle cells (Nishimura et al., 2012), and tube extension (Croce et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nishimura et al., 2012 and Croce et al., 2006.

claim: Organizing signals such as WNT can induce and orient PCP within the apical plane.
source: As organizing signals such as WNT can induce and orient PCP (Chu and Sokol, 2016) within the apical plane
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chu and Sokol, 2016.

claim: In the model, cells start to rearrange, the bottom flattens and bends inward when an external force is applied to reorient AB polarity.
source: As a result, cells start to rearrange, the bottom flattens (Figure 7B) and bends inward (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7B-C.

claim: The convergent extension driven by PCP causes the invaginated cells to rearrange, tube elongates, and merges with the top of the sphere.
source: Subsequently, the CE-driven by PCP causes the invaginated cells to rearrange, tube elongates, and merges with the top of the sphere (Figure 7F and Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7F and Figure 7—video 1.

claim: In line with experimental observations, the tube elongates due to cells moving in the tube.
source: In line with experimental observations, the tube elongates due to cells moving in the tube (Martik and McClay, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martik and McClay, 2017.

claim: In the model, two potential mechanisms behind the emergence of folds in pancreatic organoids – matrigel resistance and rapid, out-of-equilibrium, cell proliferation – will result in distinct morphologies.
source: First, we predict that two potential mechanisms behind the emergence of folds in pancreatic organoids – matrigel resistance and rapid, out-of-equilibrium, cell proliferation – will result in distinct morphologies.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: In case of rapid proliferation, the growing structure will develop many shallow folds close to the surface which later tend to deepen.
source: Our results suggest that in case of rapid proliferation, the growing structure will develop many shallow folds close to the surface which later tend to deepen.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: External pressure causes fewer but deeper and longer folds.
